1.   Consider a 3-player game in which player 1 chooses between U and D, player 2
chooses between L and R, and player 3 chooses between A and B. The payoff

matrix of this three-player game is illustrated below. Thus if 1 plays U, 2 plays R
and 3 plays B, the payoffs they earn are (1, 6, 1). Describe all the Nash equilibria
of this game? 
L   R   L   R
U   7, 7, 1   1, 8, 2   U   7, 7, 0   1, 6, 1
D   8, 1, 2   2, 2, 0   D   6, 1, 1   0, 0, 1 
A   B 
[2 points] 
2.   Consider the Traveler’s Dilemma game.
(a)   Suppose that both players become moral in the sense of becoming ‘utilitarian’. A
utilitarian is a person who tries to maximize the total amount of money (or payoff)

earned by all the players (in this case, both players). Describe all the Nash
equilibria of this transformed game.
(b)   Suppose now player 1 is selfish (maximizes his own income) but player 2 is
utilitarian (she maximizes the total income earned by the two players). Describe
the Nash equilibrium of this game.
[For both parts, (a) and (b), it may help to write down the payoff matrix of a segment
of the full game—for instance, strategies, 100, 99, and 98, for each player.]
[2 + 3 points]
3.   Three friends, Anna (A), Berlin (B) and Churchill (C) plan to meet at the cinema.

However, they forget to decide whether to meet for the matinee show (M) or the
night show (N). Each must choose independently between M and N.
Case I: If all of them manage to meet at the cinema, they are happy and they get 2
utils each. If all do not manage to meet, they are unhappy and get 0 util each.
Case II: A and C have the same preference as in Case I (if all 3 meet, they get 2
utils each; if all 3 do not meet, they get 0 utils). B gets 2 utils if   only   B and A
meet. Under all other circumstances he gets zero utils.

Patrick Luo

1   Question 1: 
1.   Consider a two-player game in which each player has 4 strategies, and
hence it is a game with 16 outcomes. Is it possible to have payoffs such that all
outcomes (no matter what the players choose) constitute a Nash Equilibrium.
If not, explain why not. If yes, describe a game which has this property. Can all
outcomes be strict Nash equilibria? What is the largest number of strict Nash
Equilibria that this game can have?
Answer:

Let us start by reviewing a few definitions from class:
1.   Nash equilibria   are strategy pairs such that, for each player, their strat-
egy is the best response (you cannot do strictly better with any other
strategy) given the other player’s strategy.
2.   Strict Nash equilibria   are strategy pairs such that, for each player, their
strategy is strictly the best response (you cannot do strictly   OR   weakly
better with any other strategy) given the other player’s strategy.
To answer the first part of the question, we can imagine a 4x4 game where

every strategy pair is a Nash equilibria. This requires that each player has the
same payoff no matter their strategy. A simple example is shown below:
A   B   C   D
a   1,1   1,1   1,1   1,1
b   1,1   1,1   1,1   1,1
c   1,1   1,1   1,1   1,1
d   1,1   1,1   1,1   1,1
Table 1: A symmetric game where every strategy pair is Nash 
Aside:   One might note that the above is very symmetric and fair (everyone
is getting the same payoff). However, this need not be true for every strategy
pair to be Nash. One player could get more than the other as seen below:
1 

[PDF page 2]

A   B   C   D
a   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3
b   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3
c   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3
d   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3
Table 2: A asymmetric game where every strategy pair is Nash
Each strategy pair in the above games are Nash because every other strategy
yields the same payoff given any opposing strategy.   Consequently, we cannot
construct a game where every strategy pair is strictly Nash.
We can show this by a quick proof by contradiction.   Let us assume that
any given strategy pair is a strict Nash equilibrium.   Thus, it must be that

for a given strategy from the opposing player, let us call that   x , our payoff for
playing each of our four possible strategies is strictly greater than the others.
The contradiction flows directly, if the pair ( A, x ) (assuming we are player 1) is
a strict Nash equilibrium, it can’t be that ( B, x ) (for the same opposing strategy 
x ) is also a strict Nash equilibrium.   Thus, not every strategy pair in a game
can be a strict Nash equilibrium strategy.
Now note how I disproved the above requires that for any given opposing

player strategy, there can be at most one strictly best response to have strict
Nash equilibria.   Logically, this implies that there is at most 4 strict Nash
equilibria in a 4x4 game (i.e.   the size of the smaller of the players’ strategy
set). We can construct a game as an example of a 4x4 game with 4 strict Nash
equilibria:
A   B   C   D
a   1,1   0,0   0,0   0,0
b   0,0   1,1   0,0   0,0
c   0,0   0,0   1,1   0,0
d   0,0   0,0   0,0   1,1
Table 3: A 4x4 game with 4 strict Nash equilibria 
2   Question 2: 
2.   The Traveler’s Dilemma is a troublesome game.   Individuals seeking to do

well for themselves end up doing miserably. 
a.   Do you find the standard game-theoretic analysis and the outcome pre-
dicted by the concept of Nash equlibrium persuasive? Spell out the reasoning
behind your answer.
The question above is open ended and does not have a set answer. However,
one potential cogent response is as below:
2 

[PDF page 3]
The standard game-theoretic analysis and its outcome is convincing so far
as the strong assumptions of rationality and complete information apply.   All
players fully understand the structure of the game, understand that their oppo-

nent has an equal understanding and foresight regarding the game, and they all
have unlimited, costless time to consider the game.   Under these assumptions
the Nash equilibrium is logical and convincing.   However, as soon as we start
pulling these pillars away, and these pillars are rather strong (i.e. I would not
expect a random selection of strangers would satisfy all these conditions), the
logical Nash outcome rapidly becomes unreasonable.
For example, the Nash outcome requires rather many cycles of logic, as-
suming the opposition is willing to go through the same hoops.

In reality, an
individual may not fully rationalize all outcomes, rather settling for the first
”good enough” answer and potentially land on the highest outcome rather than
the Nash outcome.   In essence, time and mental capacity is valuable.   People
may not want to go through the hassle of thinking through the entire strategy
space for a relatively small reward (i.e. the apparently small 1 or 2 dollar incre-
ments) and thus land on a non-Nash outcome when the experiment is done in
practice. 
b.   Explain briefly, if you were playing the Traveler’s Dilemma, what strategy

you would use and explain the rationale behind your choice?
Answer:
As with part a, there is no strict answer but one cogent response is as follows:
Assuming I am playing against a random player drawn from the population
of the USA (rather than from a population of Economists or Game Theorists) I
would play 100. My strategy relies upon the irrationality of my likely opponent.
For many, the first instinct upon seeing the traveler’s dilemma is to pick a large
value; humans are naturally cooperative when the reward is not very high for

defection, and by design, the first defection earns only one percent extra on the
cooperative reward.   Consequently, I would leverage the fact that I am likely
facing someone not versed in economics and general human behavior to attempt
to achieve the cooperative outcome.
As for why I do not play 99 if that is the case; I also gloss over the fact
that monetary reward is not the only outcome under consideration.   I would
feel rather bad if someone opted to go for the cooperative play and I instantly
betrayed them. As 1 dollar is not too important for me, I am willing to sacrifice

that for the sake of my conscience. 
3   Question 3: 
3.   Consider a variant of the Traveler’s Dilemma in which each player must
choose an   even-numbered   integer from 2 to 100. The rest is the same as in the
standard Traveler’s Dilemma.   If they choose the same integer, they get that
integer in dollars as payoff. If they choose different integers, they both get the
lower integer in dollars, but with one adjustment: the one who chose the lower
integer gets an additional   $ 2 and the one who chose the higher integer has   $ 2
3 

[PDF page 4]
deducted from her payoff.

a.   Describe all the Nash equilibria of this game.
Answer:
Evidently, no asymmetric strategy pairs (i.e. pairs where one person calls a
lower value while the other a higher one) can be a Nash outcome —the person
calling a higher value is strictly worse off.   Thus, the only strategy pairs to
consider are those where both players quote the same number. In that case, we
need to check if they have any reason to deviate.   As per above, none would
deviate to a higher number.   Deviating to a lower number is at best going to
yield the same outcome (going down one increment of 2 and claiming

the 2 dollar
bonus for being the lower bid). Thus, all strategy pairs where both players play
the same value is a Nash equilibrium 
b.   Describe all the strict Nash equilibria of this game.
Following the logic from part a, most pairs are not a strict Nash equilibrium
strategy pair because a person defecting to a value one step lower is just as well
off.   This, of course, is impossible at the lower bound.   Thus the unique strict
Nash equilibrium strategy is (2,2). 
4   Question 4: 
4.   In Rosenthal’s Centipede game (described in Chapter 2 of Basu:   Prelude
to Political Economy), standard

game-theoretic analysis, based on backward
induction, predicts that players will choose “keep” at every period and so they
will end up with player 1 earning 3 dollars and 2 earning 0 dollars.   Try to
develop a cogent argument why the standard game-theoretic argument may be
flawed and why rational players may choose “pass” at least for a few times.
This question is open ended and there are many valid answers. One example
is as follows:
We may suspect that people playing the Centipede game is more interested
in regret minimization rather than the classic rational game theory analysis. In

this case, the players may want to minimize the potential loss of their strategy
and so are willing to pursue cooperation for some number of rounds as the
relative reward to continuing compared to the reward of immediate exit starts
high. Only after the pot is big and ”tempting” enough would the players begin
to consider exit. 
5   Question 5: 
Describe the Hawk-Dove game by writing down the payoff matrix of the game.
Does the game have any Nash equilibria? Which ones of those are strict Nash
equilibrium?
Let us now complicate the game a bit.   Suppose that, over and above the
two actions,

H (Hawk) and D (Dove), each player has a third option, M. M
can stand for Moderate, referring to behavior that is less aggressive than H and
4 

[PDF page 5]
more aggressive than D. If both players play M, they both get a payoff of 1. If
one of them plays M and the other something else, they both get 0.
Write down the payoff matrix of this 3-by-3 game. Describe the Nash equi-
libria of this game? Describe the strict Nash equilibria of this game.
Answer:
Recall from class:   the Dove-Hawk game has two Nash equilibria, (Dove,
Hawk) and (Hawk, Dove). Both of these are strict Nash equilibria,

neither player
can do weakly better with any other strategy through unilateral deviation. An
example of such a game is as blow:
H   D
H   -1,-1   2,0
D   0,2   1,1
Table 4: Classic Dove-Hawk Game
Now if we add a third potential strategy we have the following 3x3 game:
H   M   D
H   -1,-1   0,0   4,0
M   0,0   1,1   0,0
D   0,4   0,0   2,2
Table 5: 3x3 Dove-Hawk Modification
Here there are three Nash strategy pairs: (H,D), (D,H), and (M,M). How-
ever, a dove in either (H,D) or (D,H) is equally as well off playing M. Conse-
quently, the only strict Nash strategy pair is (M,M) in this game.

Solution Problem Set 5 Fall 2026 ECON 2801 
September 2026 
Question 1 
For each of the statements below answer true or false (assume throughout that
no mixed strategies are allowed). 
Part A 
Consider a 2-player game with non-negative payoffs. If we change the game so
that player 1 gets double what she was getting earlier and 2 gets 4-times what
he was getting earlier, then this game will have the same Nash equilibria as the
original one.
Answer: True.
If a strategy pair is Nash, it must be that for a given player they have no

strict incentive to deviate. If we simply multiply every payoff by a set positive
constant, the greater than relations are unchanged; this also works in the inverse
for multiplying by the reciprocal. Thus, the Nashes are the same. 
Part B 
Consider a 2-player game with non-negative payoffs. If we change the game so
that player 1 gets minus 2 dollars for all outcomes compared to what she was
getting in the original game, and player 2 gets half of what he was getting in the
original game, then this game will have the same Nash equilibria as the original
one.
Answer: True

Here, once again, we can imagine any Nash outcome in the game. By def-
inition, the payoff for a given player for their strategy is at least as good for
any other   P   ( s i , s ′ 
i )   ≥   P   ( s − i , s ′ 
i ), this relation remains true no matte what we
add, subtract, or multiply each side by, so long as we do not multiply by zero
or a negative value. Thus, any pre-existing Nash remains Nash. Moreover, we
can also consider multiplying the outcome game by the reciprocal constant, or
adding the negative offset coefficient; thus, any Nash in the outcome game must

also be Nash in the first game.
1 

[PDF page 2]
Part C 
Suppose people live uniformly distributed on a one-mile stretch and buy from
the nearest vendor (and choose randomly from among vendors equi-distant to
them). Three vendors (each interested in maximizing the number of people who
will buy from them) must choose a location to set up store on the 1-mile stretch.
One vendor being at the start of the mile, one in the middle, and one at the
end is not a Nash equilibrium.
Answer: True
A simple proof by contradiction:   Let us assume this is a Nash.   If this is

a Nash, no one should have incentive to deviate. However, any of the vendors
at the end can do strictly better by moving towards the midpoint of the line.
Thus, it cannot be that the proposed outcome is a Nash Equilibrium 
Part D 
In Chess, if both players had flawless minds, as soon as it was decided who will
play White and who Black, the outcome of the game would be known.
Answer: True
Proof by contradiction.   Let us assume that, with perfect information, the
outcome is unknown.   In that case, at least two of three end states must be

possible and occur with non-zero probability:   white wins, black wins, or the
game draws. We should be able to work backwards from each state to the start
of the game. There must, thus, be some point of departure in the order of play
that reaches each of the two or more potential final outcomes. The last player
who plays has strict preferences on which outcome they want (win¿draw¿loss).
Thus, the last player who decides which path the game goes down has a strict
preference and thus would not randomize. Therefore, the outcome of the game
must be certain. 
Part E

A zero-sum game cannot have a Nash equilibrium.
Answer: False
Proof by counterexample: A zero sum game requires only that the payoffs
in each cell adds to zero.   Thus, trivially, we can have a game where all cells
are identical, let’s say they contain (0,0) for simplicity. In this case all strategy
pairs are Nash equilibria. 
Part F 
In a zero-sum game every outcome can be a Nash equilibrium.
Answer: True; see above
2 

[PDF page 3]
Question 2 
Consider the Hawk-Dove game shown below (with player 1 choosing between
rows and 2 choosing between columns).
H   D
H   -1,-1   4,0

D   0,4   2,2 
Part A 
Describe the Nash equilibria of this game.
Answer: The two Nash equilibria are (H,D) and (D,H) 
Part B 
If this game was played in a sequence, with 1 moving first and 2 moving second,
what would you expect the outcome to be and why?
Answer:   We would expect the first player to always play Hawk and the
second dove.   We find this by backwards induction on the game tree.   If the
first player played Hawk, the second player would always prefer dove (0¿-1),
conversely, if the first player played Dove, the second player would prefer Hawk

(4¿2). The first player; thus, would prefer to play Hawk to get 4 instead of 0 in
the subgame perfect equilibrium. 
Part C 
Explain why the US got an advantage in the Cuban missile crisis by secretly
planning its strategy and then suddenly announcing it to the Russians.
This question is open ended, but one formulation of the answer is as follows:
The US took advantage of the Hawk-Dove structure of nuclear brinkmanship
to gain an advantage. By playing a more aggressive, threatening stance first, the
only truly viable strategy for the USSR was to back down or risk the destruction

of the world. In essence, by threatening escalation first, the USSR can respond
by escalating leading to nuclear war or backing down and losing their strategic
position in Cuba. 
Question 3 
Consider two players, who, in period 1, plays the “Prisoner’s Dilemma” game
described below, and, after seeing the outcome of this game, play the “Assurance
Game” also shown below.
Prisoner’s Dilemma
3 

[PDF page 4]
C   D
C   5,5   0,7
D   7,0   1,1
Assurance Game
A   B
A   2,2   0,0
B   0,0   1,1
Is it possible to have a subgame perfect equilibrium of this 2-period game

such that in period 1 both players choose C? If yes, describe the full equilibrium.
If not, explain why not. Keep your answer brief—just one or two sentences.
Answer: It is not possible: the maximum punishment the subsequent assur-
ance game can generate is 1 (playing (B,B) in case of any deviation compared
to (A,A) for cooperating). However, the incentive to deviate from cooperation
is 2. Thus, a collaborative outcome of (C,C) in the fist game is impossible. 
Question 4 
People live uniformly distributed all over a city shaped like a chopped isosceles

triangle, as shown below. Two vendors, 1 and 2, have to each set up a store in
the city. People buy from the nearest vendor. (If both vendors are located at
the same distance, they toss a coin).   The aim of each vendor is to maximize
the number of customers.
Does this game have a Nash equilibrium? If so, describe it. If not, explain
why not.
This game does not have a Nash equilibrium.   A Nash equilibrium in this
style of vendor game requires that they converge to a point where they split the
area or population exactly in half in every conceivable way to cut the shape. In

other words, we need a centrally symmetric point, where every line that cuts
the shape in half intersects. Such a point does not exist for a trapezoid. Thus,
a Nash equilibrium does not exist.   A player can deviate at any given point
towards one of the bisecting lines and do better, since not all bisecting lines
meet at one point. 
Question 5 
Consider the Prisoner’s Dilemma game described below:
C   D
C   4,4   -1,5
D   5,-1   0,0
4 

[PDF page 5]
Suppose this game is played infinitely many times. The players use a discount

factor   δ   to calculate the present value of return of infinite streams of income,
where 0   ≤   δ <   1. Assume that they decide to use the trigger strategy. 
Part A 
Explain in words, why if   δ   = 0, they will not be able to cooperate and play C
each time.
A variety of answers is admissible, one example is as follows:
When the discount rate equals to zero, neither player cares for the next day.
Thus, we can treat the sequence of games as games being played independently.
Consequently, the only Nash equilibrium is (D,D) in every period. 
Part B 
Calculate the smallest value of d

which will enable the two players to cooperate
and play C each time, by using the trigger strategy.   That is, the use of the
trigger strategy is a Nash equilibrium.
Answer:
Start with the discounted value of cooperation: 
P V   = 4 + 4 δ   + 4 δ 2   + 4 δ 3   +   ... 
=   4
1   −   δ 
Next look at the discounted value of deviation for the deviator: 
P V   = 5
Now we can implement the condition for non-deviation and solve for   δ 
4
1   −   δ   ≥   5
4   ≥   5(1   −   δ )
5 δ   ≥   1 
δ   ≥   1
5 
Part C 
If the above game was being played a finite number of times, say 1000 times,

explain, assuming rationality is common knowledge, the players will get a total
return of zero.
Answer: A player knowing there is a finite number of repetition recognizes
that the last game only has one possible Nash outcome: (D,D). Since the last
5 

[PDF page 6]
game’s outcome is known we can treat the game as repeating 999 times, since
the last game’s outcome is known. We then repeat this analysis backwards to
determine that players would play (D,D) in every period yielding a zero return. 
Part D 
Explain briefly why our commonsense may conflict with the formal game-theoretic

answer to part (c).
This is an open ended question; one example answer is as below:
Players seeing a long pattern of repetition may seek to minimize regret, and,
thus, choose some degree of early cooperation rather than accepting an outcome
of zero. More practically, a random individual when faced with this game may
not think so pessimistically as to assume cooperation will immediately break
down even if it is rational. In such a case, believing there is a chance for some
length of cooperation may lead to a different outcome if the belief is mutual. 
Question 6 
Consider a game like the

Centipede, except that it is infinitely long. (The two
players can go on choosing between Keep and Pass even after they have passed
100 times.) 
Part A 
Explain why both players choosing Pass every time is a Nash equilibrium.
Answer: We can approach this with a proof by contradiction.
Let us assume that both players choosing Pass every time is not a Nash
Equilibrium. Thus, one of the players must take at some period. However, this
player knows that if they Pass on this period and take the next time they have
a turn will yield strictly more for them.   Thus, they would delay taking.   As
the ga

me is infinite, this logic does not break down due to the end of the game;
thus, always Passing is a Nash Equilibrium. 
Part B 
Explain why both players choosing Keep every time is a Nash equilibrium.
Answer: this can be proven directly:
If both players always play Keep, no one player benefit from deviating. Any
deviation past the first period does not change payoffs, since the first player
already took. However, on the first turn, choosing to Pas will yield strictly less,
as player two will then immediately take.   Thus, both players choosing Keep
every time is likewise a Nash Equilibrium.

topics.title: Nash and strict Nash equilibria
topics.summary: A Nash strategy pair leaves neither player with an incentive to deviate unilaterally; strictness rules out equally good deviations. In an m×n game, the number of strict Nash equilibria is at most min(m,n); a 4×4 example attains the bound. Positive payoff scaling or adding a constant per player preserves equilibria.

They also pose Traveler’s Dilemma variants with utilitarian preferences; the supplied problem set does not provide their solutions.

1.   Consider a 3-player game in which player 1 chooses between U and D, player 2
chooses between L and R, and player 3 chooses between A and B. The payoff

matrix of this three-player game is illustrated below. Thus if 1 plays U, 2 plays R
and 3 plays B, the payoffs they earn are (1, 6, 1). Describe all the Nash equilibria
of this game? 
L   R   L   R
U   7, 7, 1   1, 8, 2   U   7, 7, 0   1, 6, 1
D   8, 1, 2   2, 2, 0   D   6, 1, 1   0, 0, 1

2.   Consider the Traveler’s Dilemma game.
(a)   Suppose that both players become moral in the sense of becoming ‘utilitarian’. A
utilitarian is a person who tries to maximize the total amount of money (or payoff)

earned by all the players (in this case, both players). Describe all the Nash
equilibria of this transformed game.
(b)   Suppose now player 1 is selfish (maximizes his own income) but player 2 is
utilitarian (she maximizes the total income earned by the two players). Describe
the Nash equilibrium of this game.
[For both parts, (a) and (b), it may help to write down the payoff matrix of a segment
of the full game—for instance, strategies, 100, 99, and 98, for each player.]
[2 + 3 points]

However, they forget to decide whether to meet for the matinee show (M) or the
night show (N). Each must choose independently between M and N.
Case I: If all of them manage to meet at the cinema, they are happy and they get 2
utils each. If all do not manage to meet, they are unhappy and get 0 util each.
Case II: A and C have the same preference as in Case I (if all 3 meet, they get 2
utils each; if all 3 do not meet, they get 0 utils). B gets 2 utils if   only   B and A
meet. Under all other circumstances he gets zero utils.

1   Question 1: 
1.   Consider a two-player game in which each player has 4 strategies, and
hence it is a game with 16 outcomes. Is it possible to have payoffs such that all
outcomes (no matter what the players choose) constitute a Nash Equilibrium.
If not, explain why not. If yes, describe a game which has this property. Can all
outcomes be strict Nash equilibria? What is the largest number of strict Nash
Equilibria that this game can have?
Answer:

Let us start by reviewing a few definitions from class:
1.   Nash equilibria   are strategy pairs such that, for each player, their strat-
egy is the best response (you cannot do strictly better with any other
strategy) given the other player’s strategy.
2.   Strict Nash equilibria   are strategy pairs such that, for each player, their
strategy is strictly the best response (you cannot do strictly   OR   weakly
better with any other strategy) given the other player’s strategy.
To answer the first part of the question, we can imagine a 4x4 game where

every strategy pair is a Nash equilibria. This requires that each player has the
same payoff no matter their strategy. A simple example is shown below:
A   B   C   D
a   1,1   1,1   1,1   1,1
b   1,1   1,1   1,1   1,1
c   1,1   1,1   1,1   1,1
d   1,1   1,1   1,1   1,1
Table 1: A symmetric game where every strategy pair is Nash 
Aside:   One might note that the above is very symmetric and fair (everyone
is getting the same payoff). However, this need not be true for every strategy
pair to be Nash. One player could get more than the other as seen below:
1 

[PDF page 2]

A   B   C   D
a   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3
b   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3
c   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3
d   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3
Table 2: A asymmetric game where every strategy pair is Nash
Each strategy pair in the above games are Nash because every other strategy
yields the same payoff given any opposing strategy.   Consequently, we cannot
construct a game where every strategy pair is strictly Nash.
We can show this by a quick proof by contradiction.   Let us assume that
any given strategy pair is a strict Nash equilibrium.   Thus, it must be that

for a given strategy from the opposing player, let us call that   x , our payoff for
playing each of our four possible strategies is strictly greater than the others.
The contradiction flows directly, if the pair ( A, x ) (assuming we are player 1) is
a strict Nash equilibrium, it can’t be that ( B, x ) (for the same opposing strategy 
x ) is also a strict Nash equilibrium.   Thus, not every strategy pair in a game
can be a strict Nash equilibrium strategy.
Now note how I disproved the above requires that for any given opposing

player strategy, there can be at most one strictly best response to have strict
Nash equilibria.   Logically, this implies that there is at most 4 strict Nash
equilibria in a 4x4 game (i.e.   the size of the smaller of the players’ strategy
set). We can construct a game as an example of a 4x4 game with 4 strict Nash
equilibria:
A   B   C   D
a   1,1   0,0   0,0   0,0
b   0,0   1,1   0,0   0,0
c   0,0   0,0   1,1   0,0
d   0,0   0,0   0,0   1,1
Table 3: A 4x4 game with 4 strict Nash equilibria 
2   Question 2: 
2.   The Traveler’s Dilemma is a troublesome game.   Individuals seeking to do

well for themselves end up doing miserably. 
a.   Do you find the standard game-theoretic analysis and the outcome pre-
dicted by the concept of Nash equlibrium persuasive? Spell out the reasoning
behind your answer.
The question above is open ended and does not have a set answer. However,
one potential cogent response is as below:
2 

[PDF page 3]
The standard game-theoretic analysis and its outcome is convincing so far
as the strong assumptions of rationality and complete information apply.   All
players fully understand the structure of the game, understand that their oppo-

nent has an equal understanding and foresight regarding the game, and they all
have unlimited, costless time to consider the game.   Under these assumptions
the Nash equilibrium is logical and convincing.   However, as soon as we start
pulling these pillars away, and these pillars are rather strong (i.e. I would not
expect a random selection of strangers would satisfy all these conditions), the
logical Nash outcome rapidly becomes unreasonable.
For example, the Nash outcome requires rather many cycles of logic, as-
suming the opposition is willing to go through the same hoops.

In reality, an
individual may not fully rationalize all outcomes, rather settling for the first
”good enough” answer and potentially land on the highest outcome rather than
the Nash outcome.   In essence, time and mental capacity is valuable.   People
may not want to go through the hassle of thinking through the entire strategy
space for a relatively small reward (i.e. the apparently small 1 or 2 dollar incre-
ments) and thus land on a non-Nash outcome when the experiment is done in
practice. 
b.   Explain briefly, if you were playing the Traveler’s Dilemma, what strategy

you would use and explain the rationale behind your choice?
Answer:
As with part a, there is no strict answer but one cogent response is as follows:
Assuming I am playing against a random player drawn from the population
of the USA (rather than from a population of Economists or Game Theorists) I
would play 100. My strategy relies upon the irrationality of my likely opponent.
For many, the first instinct upon seeing the traveler’s dilemma is to pick a large
value; humans are naturally cooperative when the reward is not very high for

defection, and by design, the first defection earns only one percent extra on the
cooperative reward.   Consequently, I would leverage the fact that I am likely
facing someone not versed in economics and general human behavior to attempt
to achieve the cooperative outcome.
As for why I do not play 99 if that is the case; I also gloss over the fact
that monetary reward is not the only outcome under consideration.   I would
feel rather bad if someone opted to go for the cooperative play and I instantly
betrayed them. As 1 dollar is not too important for me, I am willing to sacrifice

that for the sake of my conscience. 
3   Question 3: 
3.   Consider a variant of the Traveler’s Dilemma in which each player must
choose an   even-numbered   integer from 2 to 100. The rest is the same as in the
standard Traveler’s Dilemma.   If they choose the same integer, they get that
integer in dollars as payoff. If they choose different integers, they both get the
lower integer in dollars, but with one adjustment: the one who chose the lower
integer gets an additional   $ 2 and the one who chose the higher integer has   $ 2
3 

[PDF page 4]
deducted from her payoff.

a.   Describe all the Nash equilibria of this game.
Answer:
Evidently, no asymmetric strategy pairs (i.e. pairs where one person calls a
lower value while the other a higher one) can be a Nash outcome —the person
calling a higher value is strictly worse off.   Thus, the only strategy pairs to
consider are those where both players quote the same number. In that case, we
need to check if they have any reason to deviate.   As per above, none would
deviate to a higher number.   Deviating to a lower number is at best going to
yield the same outcome (going down one increment of 2 and claiming

the 2 dollar
bonus for being the lower bid). Thus, all strategy pairs where both players play
the same value is a Nash equilibrium 
b.   Describe all the strict Nash equilibria of this game.
Following the logic from part a, most pairs are not a strict Nash equilibrium
strategy pair because a person defecting to a value one step lower is just as well
off.   This, of course, is impossible at the lower bound.   Thus the unique strict
Nash equilibrium strategy is (2,2). 
4   Question 4: 
4.   In Rosenthal’s Centipede game (described in Chapter 2 of Basu:   Prelude
to Political Economy), standard

game-theoretic analysis, based on backward
induction, predicts that players will choose “keep” at every period and so they
will end up with player 1 earning 3 dollars and 2 earning 0 dollars.   Try to
develop a cogent argument why the standard game-theoretic argument may be
flawed and why rational players may choose “pass” at least for a few times.
This question is open ended and there are many valid answers. One example
is as follows:
We may suspect that people playing the Centipede game is more interested
in regret minimization rather than the classic rational game theory analysis. In

this case, the players may want to minimize the potential loss of their strategy
and so are willing to pursue cooperation for some number of rounds as the
relative reward to continuing compared to the reward of immediate exit starts
high. Only after the pot is big and ”tempting” enough would the players begin
to consider exit. 
5   Question 5: 
Describe the Hawk-Dove game by writing down the payoff matrix of the game.
Does the game have any Nash equilibria? Which ones of those are strict Nash
equilibrium?
Let us now complicate the game a bit.   Suppose that, over and above the
two actions,

H (Hawk) and D (Dove), each player has a third option, M. M
can stand for Moderate, referring to behavior that is less aggressive than H and
4 

[PDF page 5]
more aggressive than D. If both players play M, they both get a payoff of 1. If
one of them plays M and the other something else, they both get 0.
Write down the payoff matrix of this 3-by-3 game. Describe the Nash equi-
libria of this game? Describe the strict Nash equilibria of this game.
Answer:
Recall from class:   the Dove-Hawk game has two Nash equilibria, (Dove,
Hawk) and (Hawk, Dove). Both of these are strict Nash equilibria,

neither player
can do weakly better with any other strategy through unilateral deviation. An
example of such a game is as blow:
H   D
H   -1,-1   2,0
D   0,2   1,1
Table 4: Classic Dove-Hawk Game
Now if we add a third potential strategy we have the following 3x3 game:
H   M   D
H   -1,-1   0,0   4,0
M   0,0   1,1   0,0
D   0,4   0,0   2,2
Table 5: 3x3 Dove-Hawk Modification
Here there are three Nash strategy pairs: (H,D), (D,H), and (M,M). How-
ever, a dove in either (H,D) or (D,H) is equally as well off playing M. Conse-
quently, the only strict Nash strategy pair is (M,M) in this game.

Question 1 
For each of the statements below answer true or false (assume throughout that
no mixed strategies are allowed). 
Part A 
Consider a 2-player game with non-negative payoffs. If we change the game so
that player 1 gets double what she was getting earlier and 2 gets 4-times what
he was getting earlier, then this game will have the same Nash equilibria as the
original one.
Answer: True.
If a strategy pair is Nash, it must be that for a given player they have no

strict incentive to deviate. If we simply multiply every payoff by a set positive
constant, the greater than relations are unchanged; this also works in the inverse
for multiplying by the reciprocal. Thus, the Nashes are the same. 
Part B 
Consider a 2-player game with non-negative payoffs. If we change the game so
that player 1 gets minus 2 dollars for all outcomes compared to what she was
getting in the original game, and player 2 gets half of what he was getting in the
original game, then this game will have the same Nash equilibria as the original
one.
Answer: True

Here, once again, we can imagine any Nash outcome in the game. By def-
inition, the payoff for a given player for their strategy is at least as good for
any other   P   ( s i , s ′ 
i )   ≥   P   ( s − i , s ′ 
i ), this relation remains true no matte what we
add, subtract, or multiply each side by, so long as we do not multiply by zero
or a negative value. Thus, any pre-existing Nash remains Nash. Moreover, we
can also consider multiplying the outcome game by the reciprocal constant, or
adding the negative offset coefficient; thus, any Nash in the outcome game must

also be Nash in the first game.
1

Part C 
Suppose people live uniformly distributed on a one-mile stretch and buy from
the nearest vendor (and choose randomly from among vendors equi-distant to
them). Three vendors (each interested in maximizing the number of people who
will buy from them) must choose a location to set up store on the 1-mile stretch.
One vendor being at the start of the mile, one in the middle, and one at the
end is not a Nash equilibrium.
Answer: True
A simple proof by contradiction:   Let us assume this is a Nash.   If this is

a Nash, no one should have incentive to deviate. However, any of the vendors
at the end can do strictly better by moving towards the midpoint of the line.
Thus, it cannot be that the proposed outcome is a Nash Equilibrium 
Part D 
In Chess, if both players had flawless minds, as soon as it was decided who will
play White and who Black, the outcome of the game would be known.
Answer: True
Proof by contradiction.   Let us assume that, with perfect information, the
outcome is unknown.   In that case, at least two of three end states must be

possible and occur with non-zero probability:   white wins, black wins, or the
game draws. We should be able to work backwards from each state to the start
of the game. There must, thus, be some point of departure in the order of play
that reaches each of the two or more potential final outcomes. The last player
who plays has strict preferences on which outcome they want (win¿draw¿loss).
Thus, the last player who decides which path the game goes down has a strict
preference and thus would not randomize. Therefore, the outcome of the game
must be certain. 
Part E

A zero-sum game cannot have a Nash equilibrium.
Answer: False
Proof by counterexample: A zero sum game requires only that the payoffs
in each cell adds to zero.   Thus, trivially, we can have a game where all cells
are identical, let’s say they contain (0,0) for simplicity. In this case all strategy
pairs are Nash equilibria. 
Part F 
In a zero-sum game every outcome can be a Nash equilibrium.
Answer: True; see above
2

Question 2 
Consider the Hawk-Dove game shown below (with player 1 choosing between
rows and 2 choosing between columns).
H   D
H   -1,-1   4,0

D   0,4   2,2 
Part A 
Describe the Nash equilibria of this game.
Answer: The two Nash equilibria are (H,D) and (D,H) 
Part B 
If this game was played in a sequence, with 1 moving first and 2 moving second,
what would you expect the outcome to be and why?
Answer:   We would expect the first player to always play Hawk and the
second dove.   We find this by backwards induction on the game tree.   If the
first player played Hawk, the second player would always prefer dove (0¿-1),
conversely, if the first player played Dove, the second player would prefer Hawk

(4¿2). The first player; thus, would prefer to play Hawk to get 4 instead of 0 in
the subgame perfect equilibrium. 
Part C 
Explain why the US got an advantage in the Cuban missile crisis by secretly
planning its strategy and then suddenly announcing it to the Russians.
This question is open ended, but one formulation of the answer is as follows:
The US took advantage of the Hawk-Dove structure of nuclear brinkmanship
to gain an advantage. By playing a more aggressive, threatening stance first, the
only truly viable strategy for the USSR was to back down or risk the destruction

of the world. In essence, by threatening escalation first, the USSR can respond
by escalating leading to nuclear war or backing down and losing their strategic
position in Cuba. 
Question 3 
Consider two players, who, in period 1, plays the “Prisoner’s Dilemma” game
described below, and, after seeing the outcome of this game, play the “Assurance
Game” also shown below.
Prisoner’s Dilemma

Assurance Game

Is it possible to have a subgame perfect equilibrium of this 2-period game

such that in period 1 both players choose C? If yes, describe the full equilibrium.
If not, explain why not. Keep your answer brief—just one or two sentences.
Answer: It is not possible: the maximum punishment the subsequent assur-
ance game can generate is 1 (playing (B,B) in case of any deviation compared
to (A,A) for cooperating). However, the incentive to deviate from cooperation
is 2. Thus, a collaborative outcome of (C,C) in the fist game is impossible. 
Question 4 
People live uniformly distributed all over a city shaped like a chopped isosceles

triangle, as shown below. Two vendors, 1 and 2, have to each set up a store in
the city. People buy from the nearest vendor. (If both vendors are located at
the same distance, they toss a coin).   The aim of each vendor is to maximize
the number of customers.
Does this game have a Nash equilibrium? If so, describe it. If not, explain
why not.
This game does not have a Nash equilibrium.   A Nash equilibrium in this
style of vendor game requires that they converge to a point where they split the
area or population exactly in half in every conceivable way to cut the shape. In

other words, we need a centrally symmetric point, where every line that cuts
the shape in half intersects. Such a point does not exist for a trapezoid. Thus,
a Nash equilibrium does not exist.   A player can deviate at any given point
towards one of the bisecting lines and do better, since not all bisecting lines
meet at one point.

where 0   ≤   δ <   1. Assume that they decide to use the trigger strategy. 
Part A 
Explain in words, why if   δ   = 0, they will not be able to cooperate and play C
each time.
A variety of answers is admissible, one example is as follows:
When the discount rate equals to zero, neither player cares for the next day.
Thus, we can treat the sequence of games as games being played independently.
Consequently, the only Nash equilibrium is (D,D) in every period.

Part C 
If the above game was being played a finite number of times, say 1000 times,

explain, assuming rationality is common knowledge, the players will get a total
return of zero.
Answer: A player knowing there is a finite number of repetition recognizes
that the last game only has one possible Nash outcome: (D,D). Since the last
5

game’s outcome is known we can treat the game as repeating 999 times, since
the last game’s outcome is known. We then repeat this analysis backwards to
determine that players would play (D,D) in every period yielding a zero return. 
Part D 
Explain briefly why our commonsense may conflict with the formal game-theoretic

answer to part (c).
This is an open ended question; one example answer is as below:
Players seeing a long pattern of repetition may seek to minimize regret, and,
thus, choose some degree of early cooperation rather than accepting an outcome
of zero. More practically, a random individual when faced with this game may
not think so pessimistically as to assume cooperation will immediately break
down even if it is rational. In such a case, believing there is a chance for some
length of cooperation may lead to a different outcome if the belief is mutual. 
Question 6 
Consider a game like the

Centipede, except that it is infinitely long. (The two
players can go on choosing between Keep and Pass even after they have passed
100 times.) 
Part A 
Explain why both players choosing Pass every time is a Nash equilibrium.
Answer: We can approach this with a proof by contradiction.
Let us assume that both players choosing Pass every time is not a Nash
Equilibrium. Thus, one of the players must take at some period. However, this
player knows that if they Pass on this period and take the next time they have
a turn will yield strictly more for them.   Thus, they would delay taking.   As
the ga

me is infinite, this logic does not break down due to the end of the game;
thus, always Passing is a Nash Equilibrium. 
Part B 
Explain why both players choosing Keep every time is a Nash equilibrium.
Answer: this can be proven directly:
If both players always play Keep, no one player benefit from deviating. Any
deviation past the first period does not change payoffs, since the first player
already took. However, on the first turn, choosing to Pas will yield strictly less,
as player two will then immediately take.   Thus, both players choosing Keep
every time is likewise a Nash Equilibrium.

Game Theory

Problem Set 3 
[Total 25 points]
[This problem set will be graded to give you a sense of how you are doing (the score will
not be part of your final evaluation). To be graded you must upload your answer sheet on
the course canvas by 18 September.]
1.   Consider a 3-player game in which player 1 chooses between U and D, player 2
chooses between L and R, and player 3 chooses between A and B. The payoff

matrix of this three-player game is illustrated below. Thus if 1 plays U, 2 plays R
and 3 plays B, the payoffs they earn are (1, 6, 1). Describe all the Nash equilibria
of this game? 
L   R   L   R
U   7, 7, 1   1, 8, 2   U   7, 7, 0   1, 6, 1
D   8, 1, 2   2, 2, 0   D   6, 1, 1   0, 0, 1 
A   B 
[2 points] 
2.   Consider the Traveler’s Dilemma game.
(a)   Suppose that both players become moral in the sense of becoming ‘utilitarian’. A
utilitarian is a person who tries to maximize the total amount of money (or payoff)

earned by all the players (in this case, both players). Describe all the Nash
equilibria of this transformed game.
(b)   Suppose now player 1 is selfish (maximizes his own income) but player 2 is
utilitarian (she maximizes the total income earned by the two players). Describe
the Nash equilibrium of this game.
[For both parts, (a) and (b), it may help to write down the payoff matrix of a segment
of the full game—for instance, strategies, 100, 99, and 98, for each player.]
[2 + 3 points]
3.   Three friends, Anna (A), Berlin (B) and Churchill (C) plan to meet at the cinema.

However, they forget to decide whether to meet for the matinee show (M) or the
night show (N). Each must choose independently between M and N.
Case I: If all of them manage to meet at the cinema, they are happy and they get 2
utils each. If all do not manage to meet, they are unhappy and get 0 util each.
Case II: A and C have the same preference as in Case I (if all 3 meet, they get 2
utils each; if all 3 do not meet, they get 0 utils). B gets 2 utils if   only   B and A
meet. Under all other circumstances he gets zero utils. 

[PDF page 2]
2

(a)   Describe the payoff matrices for the two games (i.e., Case I and Case II).
[For each game you will need to write down two matrices, the way it is
done in Question 1.]
(b)   What are the Nash equilibria in the two games? 
[3 + 2 points]
4.   There is a straight-line city, as shown below, in which people live uniformly
spread all along the line, from point 0 to point 1.
0 ____________________________ 1
Two vendors, A and B, have to each choose a location on the line. Each vendor’s
aim is to maximize the number of her customers. Citizens can travel along the line

(in either direction). They buy from the closest vendor (and choose by coin toss if
more than one vendor is located at the same distance). As you already know, there
is a unique Nash equilibrium in this 2-player game.
(a)   Now suppose a new vendor comes to town. Is there a Nash equilibrium (in
this 3-player game)? If so, describe it; and if not, explain why not.
(b)   Go back to the assumption of there being only two vendors. Suppose now
the culture of living in high-rise buildings comes up, and the citizens live

in four high-rise apartment buildings which are built at four equi-distant
points in the city. At the extreme left (that is, at 0) we have building   a ,
then   b , then   g , and at the extreme right   d . In other words, one-fourth of the

Describe all the Nash equilibria in this game.

2026 ECON 2801 
Patrick Luo
September 2026 
1   Question 1: 
1.   Consider a two-player game in which each player has 4 strategies, and
hence it is a game with 16 outcomes. Is it possible to have payoffs such that all
outcomes (no matter what the players choose) constitute a Nash Equilibrium.
If not, explain why not. If yes, describe a game which has this property. Can all
outcomes be strict Nash equilibria? What is the largest number of strict Nash
Equilibria that this game can have?
Answer:

Let us start by reviewing a few definitions from class:
1.   Nash equilibria   are strategy pairs such that, for each player, their strat-
egy is the best response (you cannot do strictly better with any other
strategy) given the other player’s strategy.
2.   Strict Nash equilibria   are strategy pairs such that, for each player, their
strategy is strictly the best response (you cannot do strictly   OR   weakly
better with any other strategy) given the other player’s strategy.
To answer the first part of the question, we can imagine a 4x4 game where

every strategy pair is a Nash equilibria. This requires that each player has the
same payoff no matter their strategy. A simple example is shown below:
A   B   C   D
a   1,1   1,1   1,1   1,1
b   1,1   1,1   1,1   1,1
c   1,1   1,1   1,1   1,1
d   1,1   1,1   1,1   1,1
Table 1: A symmetric game where every strategy pair is Nash 
Aside:   One might note that the above is very symmetric and fair (everyone
is getting the same payoff). However, this need not be true for every strategy
pair to be Nash. One player could get more than the other as seen below:
1 

[PDF page 2]

A   B   C   D
a   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3
b   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3
c   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3
d   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3   -1,3
Table 2: A asymmetric game where every strategy pair is Nash
Each strategy pair in the above games are Nash because every other strategy
yields the same payoff given any opposing strategy.   Consequently, we cannot
construct a game where every strategy pair is strictly Nash.
We can show this by a quick proof by contradiction.   Let us assume that
any given strategy pair is a strict Nash equilibrium.   Thus, it must be that

for a given strategy from the opposing player, let us call that   x , our payoff for
playing each of our four possible strategies is strictly greater than the others.
The contradiction flows directly, if the pair ( A, x ) (assuming we are player 1) is
a strict Nash equilibrium, it can’t be that ( B, x ) (for the same opposing strategy 
x ) is also a strict Nash equilibrium.   Thus, not every strategy pair in a game
can be a strict Nash equilibrium strategy.
Now note how I disproved the above requires that for any given opposing

player strategy, there can be at most one strictly best response to have strict
Nash equilibria.   Logically, this implies that there is at most 4 strict Nash
equilibria in a 4x4 game (i.e.   the size of the smaller of the players’ strategy
set). We can construct a game as an example of a 4x4 game with 4 strict Nash
equilibria:
A   B   C   D
a   1,1   0,0   0,0   0,0
b   0,0   1,1   0,0   0,0
c   0,0   0,0   1,1   0,0
d   0,0   0,0   0,0   1,1
Table 3: A 4x4 game with 4 strict Nash equilibria 
2   Question 2: 
2.   The Traveler’s Dilemma is a troublesome game.   Individuals seeking to do

well for themselves end up doing miserably. 
a.   Do you find the standard game-theoretic analysis and the outcome pre-
dicted by the concept of Nash equlibrium persuasive? Spell out the reasoning
behind your answer.
The question above is open ended and does not have a set answer. However,
one potential cogent response is as below:
2 

[PDF page 3]
The standard game-theoretic analysis and its outcome is convincing so far
as the strong assumptions of rationality and complete information apply.   All
players fully understand the structure of the game, understand that their oppo-

nent has an equal understanding and foresight regarding the game, and they all
have unlimited, costless time to consider the game.   Under these assumptions
the Nash equilibrium is logical and convincing.   However, as soon as we start
pulling these pillars away, and these pillars are rather strong (i.e. I would not
expect a random selection of strangers would satisfy all these conditions), the
logical Nash outcome rapidly becomes unreasonable.
For example, the Nash outcome requires rather many cycles of logic, as-
suming the opposition is willing to go through the same hoops.

In reality, an
individual may not fully rationalize all outcomes, rather settling for the first
”good enough” answer and potentially land on the highest outcome rather than
the Nash outcome.   In essence, time and mental capacity is valuable.   People
may not want to go through the hassle of thinking through the entire strategy
space for a relatively small reward (i.e. the apparently small 1 or 2 dollar incre-
ments) and thus land on a non-Nash outcome when the experiment is done in
practice. 
b.   Explain briefly, if you were playing the Traveler’s Dilemma, what strategy

you would use and explain the rationale behind your choice?
Answer:
As with part a, there is no strict answer but one cogent response is as follows:
Assuming I am playing against a random player drawn from the population
of the USA (rather than from a population of Economists or Game Theorists) I
would play 100. My strategy relies upon the irrationality of my likely opponent.
For many, the first instinct upon seeing the traveler’s dilemma is to pick a large
value; humans are naturally cooperative when the reward is not very high for

defection, and by design, the first defection earns only one percent extra on the
cooperative reward.   Consequently, I would leverage the fact that I am likely
facing someone not versed in economics and general human behavior to attempt
to achieve the cooperative outcome.
As for why I do not play 99 if that is the case; I also gloss over the fact
that monetary reward is not the only outcome under consideration.   I would
feel rather bad if someone opted to go for the cooperative play and I instantly
betrayed them. As 1 dollar is not too important for me, I am willing to sacrifice

that for the sake of my conscience. 
3   Question 3: 
3.   Consider a variant of the Traveler’s Dilemma in which each player must
choose an   even-numbered   integer from 2 to 100. The rest is the same as in the
standard Traveler’s Dilemma.   If they choose the same integer, they get that
integer in dollars as payoff. If they choose different integers, they both get the
lower integer in dollars, but with one adjustment: the one who chose the lower
integer gets an additional   $ 2 and the one who chose the higher integer has   $ 2
3 

[PDF page 4]
deducted from her payoff.

a.   Describe all the Nash equilibria of this game.
Answer:
Evidently, no asymmetric strategy pairs (i.e. pairs where one person calls a
lower value while the other a higher one) can be a Nash outcome —the person
calling a higher value is strictly worse off.   Thus, the only strategy pairs to
consider are those where both players quote the same number. In that case, we
need to check if they have any reason to deviate.   As per above, none would
deviate to a higher number.   Deviating to a lower number is at best going to
yield the same outcome (going down one increment of 2 and claiming

the 2 dollar
bonus for being the lower bid). Thus, all strategy pairs where both players play
the same value is a Nash equilibrium 
b.   Describe all the strict Nash equilibria of this game.
Following the logic from part a, most pairs are not a strict Nash equilibrium
strategy pair because a person defecting to a value one step lower is just as well
off.   This, of course, is impossible at the lower bound.   Thus the unique strict
Nash equilibrium strategy is (2,2). 
4   Question 4: 
4.   In Rosenthal’s Centipede game (described in Chapter 2 of Basu:   Prelude
to Political Economy), standard

game-theoretic analysis, based on backward
induction, predicts that players will choose “keep” at every period and so they
will end up with player 1 earning 3 dollars and 2 earning 0 dollars.   Try to
develop a cogent argument why the standard game-theoretic argument may be
flawed and why rational players may choose “pass” at least for a few times.
This question is open ended and there are many valid answers. One example
is as follows:
We may suspect that people playing the Centipede game is more interested
in regret minimization rather than the classic rational game theory analysis. In

this case, the players may want to minimize the potential loss of their strategy
and so are willing to pursue cooperation for some number of rounds as the
relative reward to continuing compared to the reward of immediate exit starts
high. Only after the pot is big and ”tempting” enough would the players begin
to consider exit. 
5   Question 5: 
Describe the Hawk-Dove game by writing down the payoff matrix of the game.
Does the game have any Nash equilibria? Which ones of those are strict Nash
equilibrium?
Let us now complicate the game a bit.   Suppose that, over and above the
two actions,

H (Hawk) and D (Dove), each player has a third option, M. M
can stand for Moderate, referring to behavior that is less aggressive than H and
4 

[PDF page 5]
more aggressive than D. If both players play M, they both get a payoff of 1. If
one of them plays M and the other something else, they both get 0.
Write down the payoff matrix of this 3-by-3 game. Describe the Nash equi-
libria of this game? Describe the strict Nash equilibria of this game.
Answer:
Recall from class:   the Dove-Hawk game has two Nash equilibria, (Dove,
Hawk) and (Hawk, Dove). Both of these are strict Nash equilibria,

neither player
can do weakly better with any other strategy through unilateral deviation. An
example of such a game is as blow:
H   D
H   -1,-1   2,0
D   0,2   1,1
Table 4: Classic Dove-Hawk Game
Now if we add a third potential strategy we have the following 3x3 game:
H   M   D
H   -1,-1   0,0   4,0
M   0,0   1,1   0,0
D   0,4   0,0   2,2
Table 5: 3x3 Dove-Hawk Modification
Here there are three Nash strategy pairs: (H,D), (D,H), and (M,M). How-
ever, a dove in either (H,D) or (D,H) is equally as well off playing M. Conse-
quently, the only strict Nash strategy pair is (M,M) in this game.

Question 1 
For each of the statements below answer true or false (assume throughout that
no mixed strategies are allowed). 
Part A 
Consider a 2-player game with non-negative payoffs. If we change the game so
that player 1 gets double what she was getting earlier and 2 gets 4-times what
he was getting earlier, then this game will have the same Nash equilibria as the
original one.
Answer: True.
If a strategy pair is Nash, it must be that for a given player they have no

strict incentive to deviate. If we simply multiply every payoff by a set positive
constant, the greater than relations are unchanged; this also works in the inverse
for multiplying by the reciprocal. Thus, the Nashes are the same. 
Part B 
Consider a 2-player game with non-negative payoffs. If we change the game so
that player 1 gets minus 2 dollars for all outcomes compared to what she was
getting in the original game, and player 2 gets half of what he was getting in the
original game, then this game will have the same Nash equilibria as the original
one.
Answer: True

Here, once again, we can imagine any Nash outcome in the game. By def-
inition, the payoff for a given player for their strategy is at least as good for
any other   P   ( s i , s ′ 
i )   ≥   P   ( s − i , s ′ 
i ), this relation remains true no matte what we
add, subtract, or multiply each side by, so long as we do not multiply by zero
or a negative value. Thus, any pre-existing Nash remains Nash. Moreover, we
can also consider multiplying the outcome game by the reciprocal constant, or
adding the negative offset coefficient; thus, any Nash in the outcome game must

also be Nash in the first game.
1 

[PDF page 2]
Part C 
Suppose people live uniformly distributed on a one-mile stretch and buy from
the nearest vendor (and choose randomly from among vendors equi-distant to
them). Three vendors (each interested in maximizing the number of people who
will buy from them) must choose a location to set up store on the 1-mile stretch.
One vendor being at the start of the mile, one in the middle, and one at the
end is not a Nash equilibrium.
Answer: True
A simple proof by contradiction:   Let us assume this is a Nash.   If this is

a Nash, no one should have incentive to deviate. However, any of the vendors
at the end can do strictly better by moving towards the midpoint of the line.
Thus, it cannot be that the proposed outcome is a Nash Equilibrium 
Part D 
In Chess, if both players had flawless minds, as soon as it was decided who will
play White and who Black, the outcome of the game would be known.
Answer: True
Proof by contradiction.   Let us assume that, with perfect information, the
outcome is unknown.   In that case, at least two of three end states must be

possible and occur with non-zero probability:   white wins, black wins, or the
game draws. We should be able to work backwards from each state to the start
of the game. There must, thus, be some point of departure in the order of play
that reaches each of the two or more potential final outcomes. The last player
who plays has strict preferences on which outcome they want (win¿draw¿loss).
Thus, the last player who decides which path the game goes down has a strict
preference and thus would not randomize. Therefore, the outcome of the game
must be certain. 
Part E

A zero-sum game cannot have a Nash equilibrium.
Answer: False
Proof by counterexample: A zero sum game requires only that the payoffs
in each cell adds to zero.   Thus, trivially, we can have a game where all cells
are identical, let’s say they contain (0,0) for simplicity. In this case all strategy
pairs are Nash equilibria. 
Part F 
In a zero-sum game every outcome can be a Nash equilibrium.
Answer: True; see above
2

Consider the Hawk-Dove game shown below (with player 1 choosing between
rows and 2 choosing between columns).
H   D
H   -1,-1   4,0

D   0,4   2,2 
Part A 
Describe the Nash equilibria of this game.
Answer: The two Nash equilibria are (H,D) and (D,H) 
Part B 
If this game was played in a sequence, with 1 moving first and 2 moving second,
what would you expect the outcome to be and why?
Answer:   We would expect the first player to always play Hawk and the
second dove.   We find this by backwards induction on the game tree.   If the
first player played Hawk, the second player would always prefer dove (0¿-1),
conversely, if the first player played Dove, the second player would prefer Hawk

(4¿2). The first player; thus, would prefer to play Hawk to get 4 instead of 0 in
the subgame perfect equilibrium. 
Part C 
Explain why the US got an advantage in the Cuban missile crisis by secretly
planning its strategy and then suddenly announcing it to the Russians.
This question is open ended, but one formulation of the answer is as follows:
The US took advantage of the Hawk-Dove structure of nuclear brinkmanship
to gain an advantage. By playing a more aggressive, threatening stance first, the
only truly viable strategy for the USSR was to back down or risk the destruction

of the world. In essence, by threatening escalation first, the USSR can respond
by escalating leading to nuclear war or backing down and losing their strategic
position in Cuba. 
Question 3 
Consider two players, who, in period 1, plays the “Prisoner’s Dilemma” game
described below, and, after seeing the outcome of this game, play the “Assurance
Game” also shown below.
Prisoner’s Dilemma

Is it possible to have a subgame perfect equilibrium of this 2-period game

such that in period 1 both players choose C? If yes, describe the full equilibrium.
If not, explain why not. Keep your answer brief—just one or two sentences.
Answer: It is not possible: the maximum punishment the subsequent assur-
ance game can generate is 1 (playing (B,B) in case of any deviation compared
to (A,A) for cooperating). However, the incentive to deviate from cooperation
is 2. Thus, a collaborative outcome of (C,C) in the fist game is impossible. 
Question 4 
People live uniformly distributed all over a city shaped like a chopped isosceles

triangle, as shown below. Two vendors, 1 and 2, have to each set up a store in
the city. People buy from the nearest vendor. (If both vendors are located at
the same distance, they toss a coin).   The aim of each vendor is to maximize
the number of customers.
Does this game have a Nash equilibrium? If so, describe it. If not, explain
why not.
This game does not have a Nash equilibrium.   A Nash equilibrium in this
style of vendor game requires that they converge to a point where they split the
area or population exactly in half in every conceivable way to cut the shape. In

other words, we need a centrally symmetric point, where every line that cuts
the shape in half intersects. Such a point does not exist for a trapezoid. Thus,
a Nash equilibrium does not exist.   A player can deviate at any given point
towards one of the bisecting lines and do better, since not all bisecting lines
meet at one point.

Players seeing a long pattern of repetition may seek to minimize regret, and,

Explain why both players choosing Pass every time is a Nash equilibrium.
Answer: We can approach this with a proof by contradiction.

Equilibrium. Thus, one of the players must take at some period. However, this
player knows that if they Pass on this period and take the next time they have
a turn will yield strictly more for them.   Thus, they would delay taking.   As

deviation past the first period does not change payoffs, since the first player
already took. However, on the first turn, choosing to Pas will yield strictly less,
as player two will then immediately take.   Thus, both players choosing Keep
every time is likewise a Nash Equilibrium.

topics.title: Nash and strict Nash equilibrium
topics.summary: A Nash strategy pair gives each player a best response; strict Nash requires a strictly best response. Every outcome can be Nash when players are indifferent, but for an m×n game there are at most min(m,n) strict equilibria: each opposing strategy allows at most one strictly best response. Positive scaling or adding a constant to a player’s payoffs preserves Nash equilibria.

topics.title: Coordination, social preferences, and Hawk–Dove
topics.summary: The materials pose cinema coordination games, a parameterized Prisoner’s Dilemma/assurance game, and Traveler’s Dilemma with utilitarian preferences, but the Problem Set 3 excerpts give no solutions. In Hawk–Dove, (H,D) and (D,H) are Nash equilibria; adding M yields (H,D), (D,H), and (M,M), with only (M,M) strict in the supplied example.

topics.title: Traveler’s Dilemma and behavior
topics.summary: In the even-bid variant with a $2 adjustment, every equal-bid pair is Nash and (2,2) is the unique strict equilibrium. The solutions also discuss how assumptions about rationality, reasoning, and regret may affect behavior; Problem Set 3 asks about utilitarian preferences but supplies no answer.

topics.title: Vendor location games
topics.summary: Problem Set 3 asks about three vendors on a uniformly populated line and two vendors serving four equally populated points; its excerpts do not give outcomes. For the chopped-isosceles-triangle city, the supplied solution says no equilibrium exists because no point lies on every population-bisecting line.

topics.title: Sequential and repeated-game incentives
topics.summary: In sequential Hawk–Dove, backward induction predicts the first player chooses H and the second D. In the repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma example, trigger cooperation requires δ ≥ 1/5; finite repetition with common knowledge of rationality unravels to (D,D). The infinite Centipede example permits both always-Pass and always-Keep as Nash equilibria.
